solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Sewage dumpers presenting basic element concerns

parts.note: one of the four classical elements

explanation.surface: A swipe at the firms pumping sewage into Britain's rivers and seas.
explanation.walkthrough: "Concerns" reads as worries, but here it is the business sense, as in a going concern.
explanation.definitionFit: British water firms have been widely condemned for releasing untreated sewage into rivers and the sea.

clue.text: Dog owner abandoned Rottweiler's lead — criminal

indicators.note: abandoned as in wild and unrestrained, so the letters run riot

explanation.surface: A dog owner walks off, leaving the Rottweiler's lead behind, and is branded a criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: "Abandoned" looks like a verb about leaving the dog; it is the adjective meaning wild, telling you to mix the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrongdoer is someone who breaks the law.

clue.text: Balls-up on standing order for body part

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom
in a down clue, on means placed above the next piece

parts.note: balls is slang for nonsense, as is rot
standard abbreviation for a standing order

explanation.surface: A bank's standing order has gone wrong, and a body part is somehow involved.
explanation.walkthrough: "Balls-up" reads as one word for a blunder; split it into balls (nonsense) and up. A standing order is a regular automatic bank payment.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain category relation: the trunk, minus head and limbs, is one part of the body.

clue.text: Republican puts on a face, heading away from the centre

indicators.note: the Republican goes first and the other pieces are added after

parts.note: the face of a clock or watch

explanation.surface: A Republican politician puts on a public face and moves away from the political centre.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about a politician drifting from the centre ground; the last phrase is really a geometric definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Radial lines run outwards from a centre, like spokes of a wheel.

clue.text: see 19ac.
Business incurs penalty (restricting legislation)

indicators.note: the penalty hems in the legislation

explanation.surface: A business is fined because of a new law restricting what it can do.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets make the second half look like an aside; it is the wordplay. "Incurs" is only the link, pointing from definition to penalty.
explanation.definitionFit: A practice is a professional business, such as a medical or legal practice.

clue.text: Latest exposure of member's programme intervention

parts.note: to flash is to expose oneself indecently

explanation.surface: A cheeky report on an MP's latest indecent exposure, broadcast as breaking news.
explanation.walkthrough: "Member" suggests an MP, but here it is the body part; the 's stands for is, joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A newsflash interrupts a scheduled programme with urgent news.

clue.text: Pressure off Lords member? That is strange

indicators.note: the letter for pressure comes off the word

parts.note: a member of the House of Lords

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether it is odd that a peer has escaped some pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: The House of Lords is the upper chamber of the UK Parliament; its members are peers. IE abbreviates the Latin id est.
explanation.definitionFit: Eerie means strange in an unsettling way.

clue.text: Appalling hospital alternative (free)

parts.note: the word that offers an alternative

explanation.surface: A grim verdict on the alternative to paid hospital care: free treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a debate on free healthcare; in fact each word is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Horrid and appalling both mean very bad.

clue.text: Two make out, holding end of plonker, pulling together

indicators.note: out as in wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged
the letters of the first words take in the extra letter

explanation.surface: Two people snog, one of them a fool, apparently in harmony.
explanation.walkthrough: "Make out" looks like a phrase for kissing; split it, since out is the signal to rearrange. A plonker is British slang for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Teamwork is people pulling together towards a shared goal.

clue.text: Clueless, go in shift to rave

indicators.note: shift means move the letters around

parts.note: the letters of go in, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone with no idea turns up to a work shift expecting a party.
explanation.walkthrough: "Rave" suggests a party, but it is the verb meaning to rant.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignorant means lacking knowledge, which is what clueless means.

clue.text: Those people concealing criminal charge get treatment

indicators.note: the people word hides the charge inside it

parts.note: a rap is a charge, as in taking the rap

explanation.surface: People covering up a crime are sent for treatment rather than punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: "Get treatment" reads as a verb phrase; get is only the link, and treatment alone is the noun definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a course of therapy is a course of treatment, whether for body or mind.

clue.text: Rees-Mogg type on drugs? Sweet!

indicators.note: the drugs follow on after the first piece

parts.note: a toff is an upper-class person
E is ecstasy, so two of them

explanation.surface: Jacob Rees-Mogg on ecstasy, and someone finds that delightful.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacob Rees-Mogg is a famously posh Conservative politician; a toff is British slang for such a person. "Sweet!" looks like an exclamation but is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Toffee is a chewy sweet made from boiled sugar and butter.

clue.text: Travel book from the pen of … Angela Rayner according to her detractors?

definitions.text: Angela Rayner according to her detractors
definitions.note: The definition names a person; the answer is the adjective her critics apply to her.

parts.note: a book is by its author

explanation.surface: A title card for a travel book supposedly written by Labour's Angela Rayner.
explanation.walkthrough: Angela Rayner is an outspoken Labour politician. Gobby is British slang for loud-mouthed. The ellipsis sets up a fake book credit.
explanation.definitionFit: Critics call Rayner gobby, meaning loud and mouthy, so her name stands in for the word by example.

clue.text: Polish alien, automatic meals on wheels provider?

parts.note: an automatic is a car with automatic gears

explanation.surface: A Polish immigrant runs an automated service delivering meals to the elderly.
explanation.walkthrough: "Polish" is capitalised to look like the nationality. Meals on wheels is a delivery service for the housebound; here the wheels belong to a train.
explanation.definitionFit: A buffet car is a railway carriage serving food, so it literally provides meals on wheels.

clue.text: Possibly old-fashioned ex-vice president drinks 'right' tea

indicators.note: the ex-vice president takes the other letters inside

parts.note: Mike Pence, former US vice president

explanation.surface: Mike Pence, perhaps a bit fusty, sips the correct sort of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: "Possibly" looks like a hedge on the surface; with old-fashioned it is the definition, flagging that the answer is archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Perchance is an archaic word for possibly or perhaps.

clue.text: Very quarrelsome whip, Dan upset Harry

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the name's letters are rearranged

parts.note: to harry is to dog, to pursue

explanation.surface: A party whip named Dan has upset someone called Harry in a fierce row.
explanation.walkthrough: "Whip" suggests a parliamentary whip, and Harry a name; both are ordinary words. The cat is a whip used for flogging.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat-and-dog relationship is one of constant fighting.

clue.text: Party's declared policy that's of use to an oil company?

definitions.meaning: the set of policies a party stands on

definitions.text: of use to an oil company
definitions.meaning: an offshore rig for drilling oil

explanation.surface: A dig at a political party whose manifesto suits the oil industry.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence about lobbying; the second half is a separate, literal definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A platform is a party's set of policies, and an oil platform is a rig for drilling at sea.

clue.text: Battle time: far right gala disrupted

indicators.note: disrupted means thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: far, R for right and gala, rearranged

explanation.surface: A call to arms as a far-right rally is broken up.
explanation.walkthrough: "Far right" looks like the political phrase; take far as written and right as R.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Trafalgar, Nelson's 1805 victory over the French and Spanish fleets, is one famous battle.

clue.text: (& 4dn.) It offers a poor view of WASP leader declared to be gay

parts.note: WASP stands for a phrase whose first word is a colour, so its leader is that colour

explanation.surface: A take on the prejudiced leader of a white Protestant group being outed.
explanation.walkthrough: "Leader" usually means the first letter; here it is the whole first word that W stands for.
explanation.definitionFit: A whiteout is a weather condition of snow and cloud where visibility falls to almost nothing.

clue.text: Conservative hack in spot — "Withdraw!"

indicators.note: the Conservative and the hack go in the spot

parts.note: a hack is a journalist; ED is an editor

explanation.surface: A Tory journalist in a tight spot is told to back out.
explanation.walkthrough: "Spot" looks like a noun, a tight spot; it is the verb, to see.
explanation.definitionFit: To secede is to withdraw formally from a union or body.

clue.text: Finished with whip and cheerful

indicators.note: the second piece comes along with the first

explanation.surface: Someone done with the whip is in a good mood.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs finishing and cheerfulness as one mood; each is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, borrowed from music: the upbeat is the lively unaccented beat before the bar line.

clue.text: 1000 escapes from state prison, causing alarm

indicators.note: the letter for 1000 leaves the words

parts.note: British slang for a prison or police station
K for kilo, a thousand, removed

explanation.surface: A mass breakout of a thousand inmates from a state jail sets off the alarms.
explanation.walkthrough: 1000 is usually M; here it is K, as in kilo, and that is what leaves. Nick is British slang for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the noun: both name a sudden rush of fear, and causing alarm is causing a panic.

clue.text: Flourishing, with new leader giving way

indicators.note: the first letter is swapped for a different one

parts.note: to flourish a sword is to wield it

explanation.surface: Someone thriving under a new boss decides to back down.
explanation.walkthrough: "Flourishing" reads as thriving; it is brandishing. The clue does not name the new first letter: the definition supplies it.
explanation.definitionFit: Yielding means giving way, as traffic yields at a junction.

clue.text: What King Brian might do with controversial technology for the city

explanation.surface: A satirical King Brian knighting chatbots for a desert city.
explanation.walkthrough: A king dubs someone a knight with a tap of the sword.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubai is a city in the United Arab Emirates.

clue.text: Kill Roger and Nick

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to murder someone, in gangster slang
second meaning: British slang for having sex with someone
third meaning: British slang for stealing something

explanation.surface: A hitman's instructions: bump off two men called Roger and Nick.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger and Nick look like names, but both are British slang verbs: to roger is to have sex with, to nick is to steal. Three separate meanings share one phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang phrasal verb covers murdering, bedding and stealing, so each clue word is a separate sense of it.

clue.text: Kitty gets end away for entertainment

indicators.note: the last letter is sent away

parts.note: a kitty is a pool of money

explanation.surface: A saucy line about someone called Kitty having sex for the fun of it.
explanation.walkthrough: "Gets his end away" is British slang for having sex; here it just means lose the last letter. Kitty is the money pot, not a name.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: doing something for fun is doing it for entertainment.

clue.text: Cyclops is about to get stiff — that's manifest

indicators.note: about as in about-turn: the piece before it faces the other way

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of an impending erection and calls it plain to see.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the setter of this puzzle, so he is ME. "Manifest" is the verb, to give form to.
explanation.definitionFit: To embody something is to manifest it in visible form.

clue.text: Roger's involved with menacing — a tabloid specialism

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A threatening Roger turns out to be tabloid territory.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is the two words either side of involved with.
explanation.definitionFit: Scaremongering, spreading alarm, is a staple of Britain's tabloid press.
